title: Cosmic Hide-and-Seek: Scientists Find the Universe's Missing Matter!
summary: Did you know most of the universe's ordinary matter is missing? Not dark matter—the mysterious invisible stuff—but the regular atoms that make up stars, planets, and even you! Scientists knew how much ordinary matter existed right after the Big Bang. But when they added up all the stars and galaxies they could see, a huge chunk was gone. It was like baking a cake with 10 cups of flour, but only finding one cup in the finished cake. Where did the rest go? Now, a team from MIT has solved the mystery using fast radio bursts, or FRBs. These are super-bright, super-short flashes of radio waves from faraway galaxies. They last only a millisecond—that's a thousandth of a second! As an FRB zooms through space, it passes through clouds of matter. The matter slows down the radio waves, stretching the flash out in time. Scientists call this "smearing." The more matter the signal passes through, the more smeared it gets. The MIT team measured the smearing of thousands of FRBs detected by a giant radio telescope in Canada called CHIME. Then they compared each smeared signal with a map of millions of galaxies. By doing this, they could figure out how much smearing came from the galaxies themselves, and how much came from the missing matter between them. What they found was amazing. The missing matter forms enormous, thin clouds around groups of galaxies. These clouds are much bigger than anyone expected—like a fog that stretches far beyond the galaxy's edge. "Where there are more galaxies, there tends to be more missing matter around them," said Haochen Wang, a graduate student at MIT. The discovery suggests that black holes and exploding stars are more violent than we thought. They fling matter out of galaxies with incredible force, pushing it into these vast halos. So next time you look at the night sky, remember: between those twinkling stars, there's a hidden universe of thin, ghostly clouds, finally revealed by flashes of radio light.
why_it_matters: This discovery helps us understand what the universe is made of and how everything is connected, just like figuring out a giant cosmic puzzle.

background_read: The Big Bang is the name for the explosion that created the universe almost 14 billion years ago, and it left behind all the matter we have today.
MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) is a top university in the United States where many scientists work on solving space mysteries.
CHIME is a large radio telescope in Canada that listens for faint signals from space, like the fast radio bursts used in this study.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists from MIT, led by graduate student Haochen Wang.
WHAT: They discovered that missing ordinary matter forms giant, thin clouds around groups of galaxies.
WHERE: In deep space, surrounding galaxies, measured with a radio telescope in Canada.
WHY: To solve the puzzle of why most ordinary matter could not be seen, even though we knew it existed from the Big Bang.
